Some notes after 6 months of using AI coding assistants on a 400k-line Rails monolith, since most takes I see are either "it's useless" or "engineers are done":

- It's great at the boring 30%: migrations, test scaffolding, converting our old jQuery widgets to Stimulus. That alone saves me maybe 4-5 hours a week.
- It's bad at anything that depends on knowing why our code is weird. It will happily "fix" a deliberate N+1 that exists because of a caching quirk from 2019.
- Review load went UP. Juniors open bigger PRs now. We added a soft 400-line limit and it helped.
- Biggest win was unexpected: writing the prompt forces me to write down what I actually want, which is a spec I never would have written otherwise.
- I've stopped using it for anything touching billing. Two subtle rounding bugs in one month was enough.

Net: I'd be annoyed if you took it away, but it's a power tool, not a coworker. Happy to answer questions about the setup.

text:
I've been asked a lot this week why I'm supporting the school phone-storage bill (SB 412) when I usually vote against state mandates on districts. Fair question, so here's my reasoning, and where I think the bill is still weak.

Why I'm for it:

1. The district-by-district approach has been tried. Our county has 14 districts; 3 adopted bell-to-bell storage on their own. Those 3 reported fewer discipline referrals in year one (numbers are in the committee packet, pp. 31–40). The other 11 said they wanted to but couldn't absorb the parent backlash alone. That's a coordination problem, which is exactly what state policy is for.

2. Teachers asked for it. Not unanimously, but the union survey was 71% in favor, and the comments were overwhelmingly about enforcement fatigue, not ideology.

3. It's cheap. The fiscal note is $4.2M statewide, mostly pouches and lockers.

Where it's weak:

- The emergency-contact provision is vague. Parents are right to worry about this, and I've proposed an amendment requiring every school to publish a plan for reaching students during a lockdown.
- Students with medical devices that run on phones (glucose monitors, etc.) need an explicit carve-out, not "at the principal's discretion."
- There's no sunset or review. I want a 3-year review with real data.

If you disagree, I genuinely want to hear it. Reply here or email the office. I read everything, even the mean ones. 🙂
link: legislature.gov · SB 412: Student Device Storage Act (full text)
